```{r}
  tibble(group  = "Linkage method (sizes at k = 6)",
         check  = names(linkage_sizes),
         result = map_chr(linkage_sizes, \(x) paste(x, collapse = ", "))),
  tibble(group  = "Agreement (adjusted Rand index)",
         check  = c("Ward against k-means, all households",
                    paste0("Ward against Ward without the ", sum(!keep_hh),
                           " extreme households (n = ", sum(keep_hh), ")")),
         result = sprintf("%.3f", c(ari_kmeans, ari_trimmed))),
  tibble(group  = "Average silhouette width by segment",
         check  = sil_by_seg$segment,
         result = sprintf("%.3f", sil_by_seg$width))
)

robust_tbl |>
  gt(groupname_col = "group") |>
  cols_label(check = "Check", result = "Result")
```

```{r}
#| label: robust-values

# Look-ups for the paragraph below
complete_min <- min(linkage_sizes$Complete)
average_max  <- max(linkage_sizes$Average)
sil_weakest  <- slice_min(sil_by_seg, width)
sil_strongest <- slice_max(sil_by_seg, width)
```

@tbl-robust gives the results.

- **Six is the best number of groups once two is set aside.** From three to ten groups the average silhouette is highest at `r best_k_3up`.
- **Ward's linkage is the only one of the three that gives usable segments.** On the same distances, complete linkage leaves a group of only `r complete_min` household`r if (complete_min == 1) "" else "s"` and average linkage puts `r average_max` of the `r nrow(cluster_data)` households in one group. Neither could be turned into six campaigns.
- **Agreement with k-means is moderate.** The ARI is `r sprintf("%.3f", ari_kmeans)`, so k-means finds a similar structure but moves many households between neighbouring groups. This is a stricter and less flattering figure than the `r percent(agreement, accuracy = 0.1)` best-match share.
- **Most of the structure holds without the extreme households.** Removing the `r sum(!keep_hh)` households with a standardised value beyond 3 (@sec-prep) and clustering the other `r sum(keep_hh)` again gives an ARI of `r sprintf("%.3f", ari_trimmed)` with the original segments. Most of the structure survives, although some households change group.
- **Some segments are much sharper than others.** The average silhouette width runs from `r sprintf("%.3f", sil_strongest$width)` for the `r sil_strongest$segment` to `r sprintf("%.3f", sil_weakest$width)` for the `r sil_weakest$segment`. The first is a clearly separate group, while the second sits close to its neighbours, which matches its low k-means agreement above.

So the six segments have real cores, but their borders are not sharp, and the weakest segments should be read as tendencies rather than fixed types.

## Describing each group (2d)

```{r}
#| label: tbl-segment-means
#| tbl-cap: "How each segment buys bath soap, in original units, with the all-household average in the last row."

# Attach each household's segment to its original (untransformed) values
original_segment <- soap_clusters |>
  left_join(soap_clean |> select(MemberID, all_of(cluster_vars)),
            by = "MemberID")

# Group sizes and means, plus an all-households row for comparison
segment_means <- original_segment |>
  group_by(cluster, segment) |>
  summarise(households = n(), across(all_of(cluster_vars), mean),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  bind_rows(original_segment |>
              summarise(households = n(), across(all_of(cluster_vars), mean)) |>
              mutate(segment = "All households"))

segment_means |>
  select(-cluster) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(c(TotalVol, NoTrans, NoBrands), decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_percent(c(PurPromo6, PurOtherPromo, MaxBrShare), decimals = 0) |>
  cols_label(segment = "Segment", households = "Households",
             TotalVol = "Total volume", NoTrans = "Transactions",
             PurPromo6 = "Share on promo 6",
             PurOtherPromo = "Share on other promos",
             NoBrands = "Brands bought", MaxBrShare = "Share to top brand") |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_body(rows = segment == "All households"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-centroids
#| fig-cap: "Segment centroids: the mean of each standardised variable within each segment (0 = the average household)."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

soap_prep |>
  left_join(soap_clusters, by = "MemberID") |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(cluster_vars), mean)) |>
  pivot_longer(-segment, names_to = "variable", values_to = "mean_z") |>
  mutate(segment  = factor(segment, levels = segment_names),
         variable = factor(variable, levels = rev(cluster_vars))) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean_z, variable, fill = mean_z > 0)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~segment, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal[4])) +
  labs(title = "Segment centroids on the six purchase variables",
       x = "Standardised mean (0 = average household)", y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: segment-values

# Look-ups for the paragraphs below, so every number comes from the table above
seg_mean <- \(seg, col) segment_means[[col]][segment_means$segment == seg]
all_mean <- \(col) seg_mean("All households", col)
seg_size <- \(seg) seg_mean(seg, "households")
fmt_pct  <- \(x) percent(x, accuracy = 1)
fmt_vol  <- \(x) comma(x, accuracy = 100)
n_hh     <- nrow(soap_prep)

# BrOthers was not clustered on, so it is only used to profile the segments
brothers_seg <- soap_clusters |>
  left_join(select(soap, MemberID, BrOthers, MaxBrShare), by = "MemberID") |>
  summarise(brothers = mean(BrOthers), zero_max = sum(near(MaxBrShare, 0)),
            .by = segment)
brothers_of <- \(seg) brothers_seg$brothers[brothers_seg$segment == seg]
zero_of     <- \(seg) brothers_seg$zero_max[brothers_seg$segment == seg]
zero_segs   <- brothers_seg |> filter(zero_max > 0) |> arrange(desc(zero_max))
```

@tbl-segment-means gives each segment's size and average purchase behaviour in original units, with the average for all households in the last row. @fig-centroids shows the same segments on the standardised scale: bars to the right are above the average household and bars to the left are below it, so the longest bars show what makes each segment distinctive.

**Small-brand regular-price buyers** (`r seg_size("Small-brand regular-price buyers")` households, `r fmt_pct(seg_size("Small-brand regular-price buyers") / n_hh)` of the panel). These households buy close to the average amount of soap, about `r fmt_vol(seg_mean("Small-brand regular-price buyers", "TotalVol"))` units over `r round(seg_mean("Small-brand regular-price buyers", "NoTrans"))` transactions, and rarely buy on promotion (`r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Small-brand regular-price buyers", "PurPromo6"))` of volume on promotion 6 and `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Small-brand regular-price buyers", "PurOtherPromo"))` on other promotions). Only `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Small-brand regular-price buyers", "MaxBrShare"))` of their volume goes to their top named brand, well below the average of `r fmt_pct(all_mean("MaxBrShare"))`, so the eight named brands win little of their spending. Instead, `r fmt_pct(brothers_of("Small-brand regular-price buyers"))` of their volume goes to `BrOthers`, the brands outside the eight named, the highest of any segment. `BrOthers` was not a clustering variable, so this is a profiling observation. It is not evidence of loyalty either, because `BrOthers` pools many small brands and cannot show whether a household stays with one of them. Because they rarely buy on promotion, discounts are unlikely to change their habits.

**Heavy multi-brand shoppers** (`r seg_size("Heavy multi-brand shoppers")` households, `r fmt_pct(seg_size("Heavy multi-brand shoppers") / n_hh)`). This segment buys the most soap, about `r fmt_vol(seg_mean("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "TotalVol"))` units, which is `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "TotalVol") / all_mean("TotalVol") - 1)` more than the average household, and buys most often, with about `r round(seg_mean("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "NoTrans"))` transactions against an average of `r round(all_mean("NoTrans"))`. They spread their volume over the most brands (`r round(seg_mean("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "NoBrands"), 1)` on average against `r round(all_mean("NoBrands"), 1)` overall) with only `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "MaxBrShare"))` going to their top brand. Their volume is large but divided between brands, so reward schemes that encourage them to keep buying the same brand suit this segment.

**Light occasional buyers** (`r seg_size("Light occasional buyers")` households, `r fmt_pct(seg_size("Light occasional buyers") / n_hh)`). These households buy very little, about `r fmt_vol(seg_mean("Light occasional buyers", "TotalVol"))` units over only `r round(seg_mean("Light occasional buyers", "NoTrans"), 1)` transactions, only `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Light occasional buyers", "TotalVol") / all_mean("TotalVol"))` of the average volume. They did not buy on promotion at all and bought the fewest brands (`r round(seg_mean("Light occasional buyers", "NoBrands"), 1)` against `r round(all_mean("NoBrands"), 1)`). Given their small volume they should be a low priority for promotion spending.

**Loyal regular-price buyers** (`r seg_size("Loyal regular-price buyers")` households, `r fmt_pct(seg_size("Loyal regular-price buyers") / n_hh)`). These households buy slightly more than average, about `r fmt_vol(seg_mean("Loyal regular-price buyers", "TotalVol"))` units, in fewer transactions (`r round(seg_mean("Loyal regular-price buyers", "NoTrans"))` against `r round(all_mean("NoTrans"))`). They give `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Loyal regular-price buyers", "MaxBrShare"))` of their volume to one brand and almost never buy on promotion (`r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Loyal regular-price buyers", "PurPromo6"))` on promotion 6 and `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Loyal regular-price buyers", "PurOtherPromo"))` on others). Since they already buy their favourite brand without discounts, reward schemes that maintain their loyalty suit them better than price promotions, which would only give away margin.

**Loyal promotion buyers** (`r seg_size("Loyal promotion buyers")` households, `r fmt_pct(seg_size("Loyal promotion buyers") / n_hh)`). This is the most loyal segment, with `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Loyal promotion buyers", "MaxBrShare"))` of volume going to one brand and only `r round(seg_mean("Loyal promotion buyers", "NoBrands"), 1)` brands bought on average. They buy an average amount, about `r fmt_vol(seg_mean("Loyal promotion buyers", "TotalVol"))` units, but `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Loyal promotion buyers", "PurOtherPromo"))` of their volume is bought on other promotions, about `r round(seg_mean("Loyal promotion buyers", "PurOtherPromo") / all_mean("PurOtherPromo"), 1)` times the average of `r fmt_pct(all_mean("PurOtherPromo"))`. Because this segment is loyal and also responds to promotions, promotions on their favourite brand suit them.

**Promo-6 buyers** (`r seg_size("Promo-6 buyers")` households, `r fmt_pct(seg_size("Promo-6 buyers") / n_hh)`). These households buy slightly less than average, about `r fmt_vol(seg_mean("Promo-6 buyers", "TotalVol"))` units, at an average frequency. They are among the least loyal, with only `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Promo-6 buyers", "MaxBrShare"))` of volume going to their top brand across `r round(seg_mean("Promo-6 buyers", "NoBrands"), 1)` brands, and `r fmt_pct(seg_mean("Promo-6 buyers", "PurPromo6"))` of their volume is bought on promotion 6, about `r round(seg_mean("Promo-6 buyers", "PurPromo6") / all_mean("PurPromo6"), 1)` times the average of `r fmt_pct(all_mean("PurPromo6"))`. Their low `MaxBrShare` is partly a small-brand effect too, since `r fmt_pct(brothers_of("Promo-6 buyers"))` of their volume goes to `BrOthers`. Promotion 6 offers timed at different points of the year suit this segment best.

**Where the `MaxBrShare` = 0 households went.** Question 1 showed that the `r nrow(zero_hh)` households with `MaxBrShare` = 0 buy only one brand, which sits inside `BrOthers`. They are not spread evenly: `r paste0(zero_segs$zero_max, if_else(zero_segs$zero_max == 1, " is", " are"), " in the ", zero_segs$segment, collapse = ", ")`. On `MaxBrShare` they look like the least loyal households, so the clustering places most of them in low-concentration segments even though each one is fully loyal to a small brand. This is the limit that Question 1 item 7 warned about, and it is one more reason the low `MaxBrShare` of the Small-brand regular-price and Promo-6 buyers should not be read as plain disloyalty.


# Question 2(e): Profiling the Groups {#sec-profile}

The segments in @sec-cluster were built from purchase behaviour only. Demographics were deliberately left out of the clustering, so that the groups describe *how* households buy rather than *who* they are. This section brings the demographics back to answer the client's next question: who are the households in each segment, and how can they be reached?

## Which three demographics, and why

Each variable was chosen because a difference between segments on it leads to a different business action (@tbl-profile-vars).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-profile-vars
#| tbl-cap: "The three profiling demographics and the business lever each one informs."

# The three demographics used to profile the segments
profile_vars <- c("SEC", "HS", "AGE")

# Missing values per profile variable (zeros were turned into NA in Section 7)
profile_missing <- soap_clean |>
  summarise(across(all_of(profile_vars), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing")

tibble(
  variable = profile_vars,
  type     = c("Ordinal, 1 high to 4 low", "Numeric, number of members",
               "Ordinal, 1 young to 4 old"),
  action   = c("Price point and value or premium range",
               "Pack size and multi-packs",
               "Media channel and message")
) |>
  left_join(profile_missing, by = "variable") |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable", type = "Type",
             action = "Business lever it informs",
             n_missing = "Missing households")
```

```{r}
#| label: other-demographics

other_missing <- soap_clean |>
  summarise(across(c(FEH, MT, SEX, EDU, CHILD, CS, Affluence),
                   \(x) sum(is.na(x))))
share_female <- mean(soap_clean$SEX == 2, na.rm = TRUE)
# Spearman correlation, because SEC is ordinal
sec_aff_cor  <- cor(soap_clean$SEC, soap_clean$Affluence, method = "spearman",
                    use = "complete.obs")
```

- **SEC (socioeconomic class)** tells a manufacturer what price a segment can bear. SEC is also one of the strata the panel was sampled on, so all `r nrow(soap_clean) - profile_missing$n_missing[profile_missing$variable == "SEC"]` households have a value and each class holds exactly a quarter of the panel, which makes any tilt within a segment easy to read.
- **HS (household size)** is the demographic most directly tied to how much soap a household uses, so it tells the client which segments suit larger packs or multi-packs. `r profile_missing$n_missing[profile_missing$variable == "HS"]` households have no size recorded and are left out of the HS summaries only.
- **AGE (age of the homemaker)** tells an advertising agency where and how to speak to each segment. Every household has a value.

**Why not the others.** `Affluence` overlaps with SEC (Spearman correlation `r round(sec_aff_cor, 2)`; SEC runs from 1 high to 4 low, so a negative value means wealthier households sit in the higher classes) and has `r other_missing$Affluence` missing households. `MT` (native language) and `CHILD` are codes with no labels in the data guide, so a difference could not be turned into an action. `SEX` barely varies: `r percent(share_female, accuracy = 1)` of homemakers with a recorded value are female. `EDU`, `FEH` and `CS` are missing for `r other_missing$EDU`, `r other_missing$FEH` and `r other_missing$CS` households and are less directly linked to a bath soap decision. @sec-profile-check tests this choice against the data.

**Missing values.** No household is dropped from the segmentation. For HS, each summary and test uses only the households that have a value, and the number used is shown.

## Profile by group

```{r}
#| label: profile-data

# Attach the three demographics (and TotalVol, to link size to volume) to each
# household's segment
profile_df <- soap_clusters |>
  select(MemberID, cluster, segment) |>
  left_join(soap_clean |> select(MemberID, all_of(profile_vars), TotalVol),
            by = "MemberID") |>
  mutate(
    # Readable labels for the ordinal codes
    SEC = factor(SEC, levels = 1:4, labels = c("1 High", "2", "3", "4 Low")),
    AGE = factor(AGE, levels = 1:4, labels = c("1 Young", "2", "3", "4 Old")),
    segment = factor(segment, levels = segment_names)
  )

# One chart function for both categorical variables, so they look the same
plot_props <- function(data, var, title) {
  data |>
    filter(!is.na({{ var }})) |>
    count(segment, {{ var }}) |>
    group_by(segment) |>
    mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) |>                 # share within each segment
    ungroup() |>
    ggplot(aes(prop, fct_rev(segment), fill = {{ var }})) +
    geom_col(colour = "white") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = pal) +
    labs(title = title, y = NULL, x = "Share of households in the segment",
         fill = NULL)
}

# Per-segment summary used in the text and in the summary table
seg_profile <- profile_df |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(households = n(),
            sec_high  = mean(as.integer(SEC) <= 2),     # SEC 1 or 2
            sec_low   = mean(as.integer(SEC) == 4),     # SEC 4
            hs_n      = sum(!is.na(HS)),
            hs_mean   = mean(HS, na.rm = TRUE),
            hs_median = median(HS, na.rm = TRUE),
            age_old   = mean(AGE == "4 Old"),
            volume    = mean(TotalVol))
```

```{r}
#| label: profile-tests-compute

# Cramer's V (Cramer, 1946): chi-squared rescaled to run from 0 to 1
cramers_v <- function(tab, stat) sqrt(stat / (sum(tab) * (min(dim(tab)) - 1)))

# Chi-squared test plus Cramer's V for one categorical variable
chisq_row <- function(data, var) {
  d   <- data |> filter(!is.na(.data[[var]]))
  tab <- table(d$segment, d[[var]])
  # simulated p-value, see below
  res <- chisq.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 5000)
  tibble(variable = var, test = "Chi-squared", n = sum(tab),
         p_value = res$p.value,
         effect = cramers_v(tab, unname(res$statistic)),
         effect_measure = "Cramer's V")
}

# only households with a recorded size
hs_df <- profile_df |> filter(!is.na(HS))

set.seed(55789)   # the simulated p-values are random, so fix them
kw_hs <- kruskal.test(HS ~ segment, data = hs_df)

profile_tests <- bind_rows(
  chisq_row(profile_df, "SEC"),
  tibble(variable = "HS", test = "Kruskal-Wallis", n = nrow(hs_df),
         p_value = kw_hs$p.value,
         # epsilon squared
         effect = unname(kw_hs$statistic) / (nrow(hs_df) - 1),
         effect_measure = "Epsilon squared"),
  chisq_row(profile_df, "AGE")
)

# Small helpers for the text
seg_prof <- \(seg, col) seg_profile[[col]][seg_profile$segment == seg]
fmt_p    <- \(p) if_else(p < 0.001, "p < 0.001", paste("p =", sprintf("%.3f",
                                                                      p)))
test_row <- \(var) profile_tests |> filter(variable == var)
```

### Socioeconomic class

```{r}
#| label: fig-profile-sec
#| fig-cap: "Socioeconomic class within each segment (1 = highest, 4 = lowest). Across the panel each class holds 25% of households."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

plot_props(profile_df, SEC, "Socioeconomic class within each segment")
```

@fig-profile-sec shows the class mix. Because the panel is stratified on SEC, every class holds 25% of households overall, so a segment that departs from a quarter in a class genuinely leans that way. The **Loyal promotion buyers** have the most lower-class households: `r fmt_pct(seg_prof("Loyal promotion buyers", "sec_low"))` are in SEC 4. Together with their high use of other promotions (@sec-cluster), this points to a budget-conscious group that stays with one brand but buys more of it when it is on offer, so price promotions *on their favourite brand* reach them well. The **Promo-6 buyers** lean the other way, with `r fmt_pct(seg_prof("Promo-6 buyers", "sec_high"))` in SEC 1 or 2 against `r fmt_pct(mean(as.integer(profile_df$SEC) <= 2))` overall: their heavy use of promotion 6 looks like a deal-seeking habit rather than a sign that they cannot afford full price, so the *timing* of promotion 6 matters more than a cheaper product. The test confirms a real but small difference (`r fmt_p(test_row("SEC")$p_value)`, Cram<U+00E9>r's V = `r round(test_row("SEC")$effect, 3)`), so SEC is a useful secondary guide, not a targeting rule on its own.

### Household size

```{r}
#| label: fig-profile-hs
#| fig-cap: "Household size within each segment (households with a recorded size only). The cross marks the mean."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

hs_df |>
  ggplot(aes(HS, fct_rev(segment), fill = segment)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 4, size = 3,
               show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal) +
  labs(title = "Household size within each segment",
       subtitle = paste0("Households with a recorded size: n = ", nrow(hs_df)),
       y = NULL, x = "Members in the household")
```

@fig-profile-hs shows household size. The **Heavy multi-brand shoppers** have the largest households (`r round(seg_prof("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "hs_mean"), 1)` members on average against `r round(mean(hs_df$HS), 1)` overall) and also buy the most soap, which fits the simple logic that more people use more soap. For a client this is the natural segment for family packs and multi-packs, ideally tied to one brand to counter their habit of spreading volume across brands. The **Small-brand regular-price buyers** and **Promo-6 buyers** have the smallest households (`r round(seg_prof("Small-brand regular-price buyers", "hs_mean"), 1)` and `r round(seg_prof("Promo-6 buyers", "hs_mean"), 1)` members), so standard packs suit them. The difference is statistically significant but small (`r fmt_p(test_row("HS")$p_value)`, epsilon squared = `r round(test_row("HS")$effect, 3)`).

One pattern needs a warning: only `r seg_prof("Light occasional buyers", "hs_n")` of the `r seg_prof("Light occasional buyers", "households")` **Light occasional buyers** have a recorded household size. The largest share of the `r sum(is.na(soap_clean$HS))` households with no household size (which also lack education, language, gender, TV and Affluence, @sec-prep) falls into this segment (`r seg_prof("Light occasional buyers", "households") - seg_prof("Light occasional buyers", "hs_n")` of them), so it may partly reflect households with incomplete panel records rather than a true customer type, so its household size profile should not be relied on. Its `SEC` and `AGE` are recorded for every household, so those two comparisons still hold.

### Age of the homemaker

```{r}
#| label: fig-profile-age
#| fig-cap: "Age of the homemaker within each segment (1 = youngest, 4 = oldest)."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

plot_props(profile_df, AGE, "Age of the homemaker within each segment")
```

@fig-profile-age shows that age does **not** separate the segments (`r fmt_p(test_row("AGE")$p_value)`, Cram<U+00E9>r's V = `r round(test_row("AGE")$effect, 3)`). Older homemakers are the largest group in every segment, from `r fmt_pct(min(seg_profile$age_old))` to `r fmt_pct(max(seg_profile$age_old))` in the oldest class, and the differences in the chart are within what chance would produce. The practical conclusion is that age gives no reason to reach one segment through a different media channel from another.

## Are the differences real?

A chart can show a difference that is only noise, so each variable is tested. SEC and AGE are categorical, so a **chi-squared test of independence** checks whether the mix of classes differs between segments. Some cells are small (few households have the youngest age code), so the p-value is simulated rather than taken from the chi-squared table, which keeps it valid when expected counts are below 5. HS is a count with a long right tail, so the **Kruskal-Wallis test**, which compares segments on ranks rather than means, is used instead of ANOVA. With `r nrow(profile_df)` households even a tiny difference can be "significant", so an effect size is also reported: Cram<U+00E9>r's V [@cramer1946] for the categorical variables and epsilon squared for HS, both running from 0 (no association) to 1.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-profile-tests
#| tbl-cap: "Do the segments differ on each demographic?"

profile_tests |>
  select(variable, test, n, p_value, effect, effect_measure) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(effect, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(p_value, decimals = 4) |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable", test = "Test", n = "Households used",
             p_value = "p-value", effect = "Effect size",
             effect_measure = "Measure")
```

@tbl-profile-tests gives the results. SEC and household size differ significantly between segments, but both effects are small, and age does not differ at all. **The segments are therefore only weakly visible in demographics.** That is a finding in itself, and it supports XYZ's move to behavioural segmentation: a client could not have found these segments from demographics alone, so targeting should run on purchase data (panel or loyalty card records), with SEC and household size used to fine-tune the offer.

The next two sections go beyond the question. They show which segments and classes cause the differences, and test whether a better demographic was left out.

## Extra check: where do the differences come from?

The tests above say *whether* the segments differ. This check says *which* segment and class cause it, so a client knows where to act. For SEC and AGE, the **standardised residual** of each cell compares the number of households in that segment and class with the number expected if every segment had the same mix. A value beyond <U+00B1>2 marks a clear excess (positive) or shortfall (negative). For HS, **pairwise Wilcoxon tests** compare every pair of segments, with the **Holm adjustment** keeping the overall chance of a false difference at 5% across all the comparisons.

```{r}
#| label: fig-profile-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Standardised residuals of segment by SEC and by AGE. Beyond plus or minus 2 is a clear difference."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Standardised residuals of the segment by class table, in long form for
# plotting
resid_df <- function(data, var) {
  d   <- data |> filter(!is.na(.data[[var]]))
  tab <- table(segment = d$segment, level = d[[var]])
  # Simulated p-value, so no small-cell warning. Only the residuals are used
  res <- chisq.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000)
  as.data.frame.table(res$stdres, responseName = "resid") |>
    mutate(variable = var)
}

plot_resid <- function(rd, title) {
  ggplot(rd, aes(level, fct_rev(segment), fill = resid)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(resid, 1), colour = abs(resid) > 2),
              show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal_ink, `FALSE` = pal_ink)) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = pal_lo, mid = "white", high = pal_hi,
                         midpoint = 0) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Residual")
}

sec_resid <- resid_df(profile_df, "SEC")
age_resid <- resid_df(profile_df, "AGE")

plot_resid(sec_resid, "Socioeconomic class") +
  plot_resid(age_resid, "Age of the homemaker")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-profile-hs-pairs
#| tbl-cap: "Household size: segment pairs that still differ after the Holm adjustment."

hs_pairs <- pairwise.wilcox.test(hs_df$HS, hs_df$segment,
                                 p.adjust.method = "holm", exact = FALSE) |>
  tidy()

hs_pairs |>
  filter(p.value < 0.05) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(p.value, decimals = 4) |>
  cols_label(group1 = "Segment", group2 = "Compared with",
             p.value = "Holm-adjusted p-value")
```

```{r}
#| label: residual-values

resid_text <- \(seg, lvl) {
  sprintf("%+.1f",
          sec_resid$resid[sec_resid$segment == seg & sec_resid$level == lvl])
}
n_age_cells <- sum(abs(age_resid$resid) > 2)
```

@fig-profile-residuals and @tbl-profile-hs-pairs show the detail. The SEC result is driven by three segments: the Loyal promotion buyers have more SEC 4 households than expected (`r resid_text("Loyal promotion buyers", "4 Low")`), the Promo-6 buyers have more SEC 2 households (`r resid_text("Promo-6 buyers", "2")`), and the small Light occasional group has more SEC 1 households (`r resid_text("Light occasional buyers", "1 High")`). `r if (n_age_cells == 0) "No age cell goes beyond 2 in either direction, which matches the non-significant age test." else paste(n_age_cells, "age cells go beyond 2 in either direction, but the age test as a whole is not significant.")` For household size, only the pairs in the table above differ after adjustment, and every one of them involves the Heavy multi-brand shoppers' larger households. These are the comparisons a client should rely on when choosing which segment gets which offer.

## Extra check: did we miss a better demographic? {#sec-profile-check}

The three variables were chosen for business reasons. As a check, every demographic is measured on how strongly it separates the segments with one common measure, Cram<U+00E9>r's V. Numeric variables (HS, Affluence and EDU, which has nine sparse levels) are first cut into four equal-sized groups, and native-language codes held by fewer than 20 households are pooled, so that rare codes do not inflate the measure.

```{r}
#| label: fig-profile-all-demographics
#| fig-cap: "How strongly each demographic separates the six segments (Cramer's V)."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

all_demo_v <- map_dfr(demo_cols, \(v) {
  d <- soap_clusters |>
    select(MemberID, segment) |>
    left_join(soap_clean |> select(MemberID, value = all_of(v)),
              by = "MemberID") |>
    filter(!is.na(value))
  grp <- if (v %in% c("HS", "Affluence", "EDU")) {
    # numeric: four equal-sized groups
    factor(ntile(d$value, 4))
  } else {
    # categorical: pool rare codes
    fct_lump_min(factor(d$value), min = 20)
  }
  tab <- table(d$segment, grp)
  # Simulated p-value, so no small-cell warning. Only the statistic is used
  res <- chisq.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000)
  tibble(variable = v, n = nrow(d),
         cramers_v = cramers_v(tab, unname(res$statistic)),
         chosen = v %in% profile_vars)
})

all_demo_v |>
  ggplot(aes(cramers_v, fct_reorder(variable, cramers_v), fill = chosen)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal_grey),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "Chosen", `FALSE` = "Not chosen")) +
  labs(title = "How strongly each demographic separates the segments",
       x = "Cramer's V", y = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: check-values

demo_v <- \(v) round(all_demo_v$cramers_v[all_demo_v$variable == v], 3)
```

@fig-profile-all-demographics shows that every demographic separates the segments only weakly (the largest V is `r round(max(all_demo_v$cramers_v), 3)`), which repeats the finding above. HS and SEC are among the stronger variables, which supports two of the three choices. `Affluence` (V = `r demo_v("Affluence")`) and `EDU` (`r demo_v("EDU")`) separate the segments more than AGE (`r demo_v("AGE")`). They were left out because Affluence largely repeats SEC and EDU has many sparse levels and more missing values. Since the brief lets the team choose any three demographics, Affluence would be an acceptable alternative to AGE. It is reported here so a reader can see the trade-off rather than take the choice on trust.


## Summary profile of each segment

```{r}
#| label: tbl-profile-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Demographic profile of each segment."

seg_profile |>
  select(segment, households, sec_high, sec_low, hs_median, hs_mean, age_old) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_percent(c(sec_high, sec_low, age_old), decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(hs_mean, decimals = 1) |>
  cols_label(segment = "Segment", households = "Households",
             sec_high = "SEC 1 or 2", sec_low = "SEC 4",
             hs_median = "Median size", hs_mean = "Mean size",
             age_old = "Homemaker AGE 4") |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Socioeconomic class", columns = c(sec_high, sec_low)) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Household size", columns = c(hs_median, hs_mean))
```

@tbl-profile-summary brings the profile together. Putting purchase behaviour (@sec-cluster) and demographics together:

- **Heavy multi-brand shoppers:** the largest households and the most volume. Family packs and multi-packs, combined with a reward scheme that concentrates their spending on one brand.
- **Loyal promotion buyers:** the most lower-class households (`r fmt_pct(seg_prof("Loyal promotion buyers", "sec_low"))` in SEC 4). Value packs and price promotions on the brand they already favour.
- **Promo-6 buyers:** more higher-class households than average (`r fmt_pct(seg_prof("Promo-6 buyers", "sec_high"))` in SEC 1 or 2). Promotion 6 offers spread through the year; a cheaper product is not needed.
- **Loyal regular-price buyers:** demographically close to the average household. Reward schemes rather than discounts, which they do not need.
- **Small-brand regular-price buyers:** close to average with smaller households, so demographics give little extra help in finding them; they are best reached through purchase data, with trial and visibility to win them from small brands.
- **Light occasional buyers:** too small, too light and too poorly recorded (`r seg_prof("Light occasional buyers", "households") - seg_prof("Light occasional buyers", "hs_n")` of `r seg_prof("Light occasional buyers", "households")` have no household size, education or TV record) to target separately.


# Question 3: Dimension Reduction with PCA {#sec-pca}

Question 2 described each household with six purchase behaviour variables. **Principal component analysis (PCA)** asks whether those six can be summarised by fewer new variables, called components, without losing much information. Each component is a weighted combination of the six: the first captures as much of the variation between households as possible, the second captures as much of what is left as possible while being uncorrelated with the first, and so on. If the six variables overlap, a few components carry most of the information, which makes the households easier to describe and to plot.

## Is PCA worth doing on these variables?

PCA can only compress variables that move together. If the six were unrelated, every component would carry about the same share and nothing would be gained.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pca-correlation
#| tbl-cap: "Correlations between the six prepared variables (the same data the clustering used)."

pca_cor <- soap_prep |>
  select(all_of(cluster_vars)) |>
  cor()

# The strongest pair, and each variable's largest correlation with any other
top_pair <- as_tibble(pca_cor, rownames = "var1") |>
  pivot_longer(-var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "r") |>
  filter(var1 < var2) |>                       # each pair once, no diagonal
  slice_max(abs(r), n = 1)

loner <- as_tibble(pca_cor, rownames = "variable") |>
  pivot_longer(-variable, names_to = "other", values_to = "r") |>
  filter(variable != other) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(max_abs_r = max(abs(r))) |>
  slice_min(max_abs_r, n = 1)

as_tibble(pca_cor, rownames = "variable") |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(-variable, decimals = 2) |>
  data_color(columns = -variable,
             palette = c(pal_lo, "#F9E1EB", pal_hi),
             domain = c(-1, 1), autocolor_text = FALSE)
```

@tbl-pca-correlation shows the correlations. The strongest relationship is between `r top_pair$var1` and `r top_pair$var2` (r = `r round(top_pair$r, 2)`), so there is real overlap for PCA to use. At the other extreme, `r loner$variable` is almost independent of the rest (its largest correlation with any other variable is `r round(loner$max_abs_r, 2)`), so it cannot be folded into the others and is likely to need a component of its own.

## Running the PCA

The PCA follows the tidymodels recipe pattern [@kuhn2020tidymodels; @R-recipes]: a recipe with `step_normalize()` and `step_pca()`, estimated with `prep()`, and checked against base R's `prcomp()`.

```{r}
#| label: pca-fit

pca_data <- soap_prep |> select(MemberID, all_of(cluster_vars))

pca_rec <- recipe(~ ., data = pca_data) |>
  # keep the ID, but leave it out of the PCA
  update_role(MemberID, new_role = "id") |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>     # see the note below
  # keep all six for now
  step_pca(all_numeric_predictors(), num_comp = length(cluster_vars),
           id = "pca") |>
  prep()

# What step_normalize learned: for already standardised data, means are 0 and
# sds are 1
norm_check <- tidy(pca_rec, number = 1) |>
  group_by(statistic) |>
  summarise(furthest = max(abs(value - if_else(statistic == "mean", 0, 1))))

# Cross-check against base R: prcomp() should give the same variances
pca_base <- prcomp(select(pca_data, all_of(cluster_vars)))
```

**Is `step_normalize()` needed again?** PCA must be run on standardised data, otherwise the variable with the largest units (volume) would dominate the first component only because its numbers are bigger. `soap_prep` was already standardised in @sec-prep, so this step changes nothing here: the means it learned differ from 0, and the standard deviations from 1, by at most `r sprintf("%.0e", max(norm_check$furthest))`, which is rounding error. It is kept so that the recipe is safe on its own if it is ever run on unprepared data. All six components are kept at this stage so that the number to retain is chosen from the evidence below rather than fixed in advance.

## How many components to keep

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pca-variance
#| tbl-cap: "Variance explained by each component."

pca_var <- tidy(pca_rec, id = "pca", type = "variance") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = terms, values_from = value) |>
  transmute(component,
            eigenvalue = variance,
            percent    = `percent variance`,
            cumulative = `cumulative percent variance`)

# The variances match base R's prcomp() (eigenvalue = sd squared)
same_as_prcomp <- isTRUE(all.equal(pca_var$eigenvalue, pca_base$sdev^2,
                                   check.attributes = FALSE))

pca_var |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(eigenvalue, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(c(percent, cumulative), decimals = 1, pattern = "{x}%") |>
  cols_label(component = "Component", eigenvalue = "Eigenvalue",
             percent = "Variance explained", cumulative = "Cumulative")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pca-scree
#| fig-cap: "Left: scree plot with the eigenvalue of 1 marked. Right: cumulative variance with the 70% line."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

# Kaiser: eigenvalue above 1
n_kaiser <- sum(pca_var$eigenvalue > 1)
# enough components for 70% of the variation
n_70     <- which(pca_var$cumulative >= 70)[1]
# the decision (explained below)
n_keep   <- n_70

scree <- pca_var |>
  ggplot(aes(component, eigenvalue)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  geom_line(colour = pal[1]) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = component <= n_keep), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal_grey)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = pca_var$component) +
  labs(title = "Scree plot", x = "Component", y = "Eigenvalue")

cumul <- pca_var |>
  ggplot(aes(component, cumulative / 100)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = component <= n_keep), show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.7, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal_grey)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = pca_var$component) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative variance explained", x = "Component", y = NULL)

scree + cumul
```

```{r}
#| label: pca-keep-values

eig      <- pca_var$eigenvalue
cum_keep <- pca_var$cumulative[n_keep]
```

@tbl-pca-variance and @fig-pca-scree show the variance explained. The first component explains `r round(pca_var$percent[1], 1)`% of the variation on its own, and each further component adds less. Three rules were read together to decide how many to keep:

1. **Kaiser rule** [@kaiser1960] (keep components with an eigenvalue above 1, meaning the component carries more information than a single standardised variable): `r n_kaiser` components.
2. **Share of variance** (keep enough components to explain at least 70% of the variation): `r n_70` components, together explaining `r round(cum_keep, 1)`%. The unit's PCA lecture suggests that more than 60% is enough for social science data such as household purchases [@etw2500pca], so 70% is the stricter of the two and both are met.
3. **Scree plot** (keep the components before the curve flattens): after component `r n_keep` the eigenvalues drop to `r round(eig[n_keep + 1], 2)` and `r round(eig[n_keep + 2], 2)`, which are almost level, so the curve flattens there.

**The three rules agree, so `r n_keep` components are retained**, keeping `r round(cum_keep, 1)`% of the information while reducing six variables to three dimensions. One caution: the third eigenvalue is `r round(eig[3], 3)`, only just above 1, so the Kaiser rule alone would be a weak reason to keep it; the share of variance and the scree plot are what make the case. As a check, base R's `prcomp()` gives `r if (same_as_prcomp) "exactly the same eigenvalues" else "different eigenvalues, which needs checking"`.

## Naming and describing the components

The **loadings** are the weights each original variable gets in a component. A loading far from 0 (here beyond <U+00B1>0.4, a common cut-off) means the variable helps define that component, and its sign says whether the variable rises or falls as the component score rises. The sign of a whole component is arbitrary in PCA (multiplying every loading by -1 describes the same component), so each component is flipped, where needed, so that its largest loading is positive and "a high score" reads naturally. @fig-pca-loadings and @tbl-pca-loadings show the loadings of the retained components.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pca-loadings
#| fig-cap: "Loadings of the three retained components. Dark bars are beyond plus or minus 0.4 and define the component."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

kept_pcs <- paste0("PC", seq_len(n_keep))

pca_load_raw <- tidy(pca_rec, id = "pca", type = "coef") |>
  filter(component %in% kept_pcs) |>
  select(variable = terms, component, value)

# Flip each component so its largest loading is positive (direction only, the
# PCA is unchanged)
pc_flip <- pca_load_raw |>
  group_by(component) |>
  slice_max(abs(value), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(component, flip = sign(value))

pca_load <- pca_load_raw |>
  left_join(pc_flip, by = "component") |>
  mutate(value  = value * flip,
         strong = abs(value) >= 0.4)

pca_load |>
  ggplot(aes(value, fct_rev(factor(variable, levels = cluster_vars)),
             fill = strong)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-0.4, 0.4), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "grey55") +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(component, levels = kept_pcs)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal_grey),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "Defines the component",
                               `FALSE` = "Weak")) +
  labs(title = "Loadings of the retained components", x = "Loading", y = NULL,
       fill = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pca-loadings
#| tbl-cap: "Loadings of the retained components (bold: beyond plus or minus 0.4)."

pca_load_wide <- pca_load |>
  select(variable, component, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = component, values_from = value) |>
  arrange(factor(variable, levels = cluster_vars))

load_gt <- pca_load_wide |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(all_of(kept_pcs), decimals = 2) |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable")

# Bold the loadings that define each component
for (pc in kept_pcs) {
  load_gt <- load_gt |>
    tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold", color = pal[1]),
              locations = cells_body(columns = all_of(pc),
                                     rows = which(abs(pca_load_wide[[pc]]) >=
                                                  0.4)))
}
load_gt
```

```{r}
#| label: pca-load-values

# Loading of one variable on one component, and a component's share, as text
loading_text <- \(v, pc) {
  sprintf("%+.2f", pca_load_wide[[pc]][pca_load_wide$variable == v])
}
pct_var <- \(pc) {
  round(pca_var$percent[pca_var$component == as.integer(sub("PC", "", pc))], 1)
}
```

**PC1: Shopping activity and brand variety** (`r pct_var("PC1")`% of the variation). It is defined by NoTrans (`r loading_text("NoTrans", "PC1")`), NoBrands (`r loading_text("NoBrands", "PC1")`) and TotalVol (`r loading_text("TotalVol", "PC1")`), so a high PC1 score means a household that buys often, buys a lot and spreads its purchases across many brands, while a low score is a light, occasional buyer. Because the number of brands loads together with the activity variables, buying more goes with trying more brands: in these data the heaviest buyers are not the most loyal ones (MaxBrShare loads `r loading_text("MaxBrShare", "PC1")`).

**PC2: Loyal bulk buying versus promotion seeking** (`r pct_var("PC2")`% of the variation). It is defined by MaxBrShare (`r loading_text("MaxBrShare", "PC2")`) and TotalVol (`r loading_text("TotalVol", "PC2")`) against PurPromo6 (`r loading_text("PurPromo6", "PC2")`). A high PC2 score means a household that puts most of its volume on one brand and buys in quantity without needing a deal; a low score means a household whose purchases lean on promotion 6. This is the loyalty versus deal-seeking axis in the Key Problem, and it is a different idea from how active a household is (PC1). The word "bulk" needs care, because TotalVol also loads `r loading_text("TotalVol", "PC1")` on PC1. So part of the volume difference between households is already counted as activity in PC1, and because the components are uncorrelated, the volume part of PC2 is the part of volume that PC1 does not already explain.

**PC3: Response to other promotions** (`r pct_var("PC3")`% of the variation). It is almost entirely PurOtherPromo (`r loading_text("PurOtherPromo", "PC3")`), the variable that was barely related to any other. It earns a component of its own because this kind of promotion response is separate from both activity and loyalty: knowing how much a household buys, or how loyal it is, says little about whether it takes up these offers.

## The households on the components

Each household gets a score on every retained component. Plotting the first two scores shows the households in two dimensions instead of six, coloured by their segment from Question 2, with the loadings drawn as arrows pointing in the direction in which each variable increases.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pca-biplot
#| fig-cap: "Households on the first two components, coloured by segment. Arrows show the loadings (stretched to be visible; only direction and relative length matter)."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6.5

# Component scores, flipped the same way as the loadings, joined to the segments
pca_scores <- bake(pca_rec, new_data = NULL) |>
  select(MemberID, all_of(kept_pcs)) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(kept_pcs),
                \(x) x * pc_flip$flip[pc_flip$component == cur_column()])) |>
  left_join(soap_clusters |> select(MemberID, segment), by = "MemberID") |>
  mutate(segment = factor(segment, levels = segment_names))

# Arrows: the PC1 and PC2 loadings, stretched so they are visible next to the
# scores
arrow_scale <- 0.8 * max(abs(c(pca_scores$PC1, pca_scores$PC2)))
pca_arrows  <- pca_load |>
  filter(component %in% c("PC1", "PC2")) |>
  select(variable, component, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = component, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(across(c(PC1, PC2), \(x) x * arrow_scale))

ggplot(pca_scores, aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = segment), alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_segment(data = pca_arrows, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")), colour = pal_ink) +
  geom_label(data = pca_arrows, aes(label = variable), size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(title = "Households on the first two components",
       x = "PC1: Shopping activity and brand variety",
       y = "PC2: Loyal bulk buying versus promotion seeking", colour = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pca-segments
#| tbl-cap: "Mean component score of each segment, and the share of each component's variation explained by segment membership."

# Mean score per segment, and R squared of each component's scores on segment
seg_means <- pca_scores |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(kept_pcs), mean)) |>
  mutate(segment = as.character(segment))

seg_r2 <- map_dbl(kept_pcs, \(pc) summary(lm(reformulate("segment", pc),
                                             data = pca_scores))$r.squared) |>
  set_names(kept_pcs)

seg_means |>
  bind_rows(tibble(segment = "Variation explained by segment",
                   PC1 = seg_r2[["PC1"]], PC2 = seg_r2[["PC2"]],
                   PC3 = seg_r2[["PC3"]])) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(all_of(kept_pcs),
             rows = segment != "Variation explained by segment",
             decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_percent(all_of(kept_pcs),
              rows = segment == "Variation explained by segment",
              decimals = 0) |>
  cols_label(segment = "Segment")
```

```{r}
#| label: pca-segment-values

seg_score <- \(seg, pc) sprintf("%+.2f",
                                seg_means[[pc]][seg_means$segment == seg])
```

@fig-pca-biplot plots the households and @tbl-pca-segments gives each segment's mean score. The plot reads like a map of the segments. **Moving right** (PC1) goes from the Light occasional buyers (`r seg_score("Light occasional buyers", "PC1")`) to the Heavy multi-brand shoppers (`r seg_score("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "PC1")`), the two ends of shopping activity. **Moving up** (PC2) goes from the Promo-6 buyers at the bottom (`r seg_score("Promo-6 buyers", "PC2")`) to the Loyal regular-price buyers (`r seg_score("Loyal regular-price buyers", "PC2")`) and Loyal promotion buyers (`r seg_score("Loyal promotion buyers", "PC2")`) at the top, the loyalty against deal-seeking axis. The MaxBrShare and PurPromo6 arrows point in opposite directions, so households that are loyal to one brand tend not to rely on promotion 6. PC3, not shown in the plot, is where the **Loyal promotion buyers** stand out (`r seg_score("Loyal promotion buyers", "PC3")`), because they are the segment that takes up other promotions.

Segment membership explains `r percent(seg_r2[["PC1"]], accuracy = 1)` of the variation in PC1, `r percent(seg_r2[["PC2"]], accuracy = 1)` in PC2 and `r percent(seg_r2[["PC3"]], accuracy = 1)` in PC3. **The PCA therefore agrees with the clustering and names the dimensions behind it:** the clustering finds the groups, and the components name the three dimensions on which they differ, which are activity, loyalty against promotion 6, and response to other promotions. This is not independent proof that the segments are real, because both methods use the same six prepared variables.

## What PCA gives up

PCA kept `r round(cum_keep, 1)`% of the information, so `r round(100 - cum_keep, 1)`% of the variation between households is set aside. Three further limits matter for a client:

- **Components are harder to explain than the original variables.** "Shopping activity and brand variety" is a weighted mix of several variables, and a manager may find "number of transactions" easier to act on. This is why the segments in Question 2 were described with the original variables.
- **PCA only finds straight-line relationships, and is pulled by extreme values.** The skew correction and standardisation in @sec-prep reduce this, but a curved pattern, or one driven by a small group of heavy promotion users, can be missed or exaggerated.
- **It cannot compress variables that do not overlap.** `r loner$variable` was nearly unrelated to the others, so it needed a component to itself. When most variables are unrelated, PCA saves little; it is most useful when many variables measure a few underlying ideas.


# Conclusion and Recommendations {#sec-conclusion}

## What we found

XYZ asked whether the bath soap market could be segmented by **how households buy** rather than by who they are. It can. Question 1 showed that raw brand shares measure *which* brand a household buys, not *how loyal* it is, so they were replaced by a single concentration measure, `MaxBrShare`. Six behaviour variables covering volume, frequency, promotion response and loyalty were then cleaned, corrected for skewness and standardised (@sec-prep), and Ward's hierarchical clustering grouped the `r nrow(soap_clusters)` households into **six segments** (@sec-cluster).

The PCA in @sec-pca agrees with the clustering and names the dimensions behind it. It is not independent proof, since both use the same six variables. Three components keep `r round(cum_keep, 1)`% of the information: **shopping activity and brand variety**, **loyal bulk buying against promotion 6**, and **response to other promotions**. Segment membership explains `r percent(seg_r2[["PC1"]], accuracy = 1)`, `r percent(seg_r2[["PC2"]], accuracy = 1)` and `r percent(seg_r2[["PC3"]], accuracy = 1)` of the variation in these three components, so the segments line up with clear, nameable dimensions of behaviour rather than with noise.

The demographic profile in @sec-profile adds one important lesson: **the segments are only weakly visible in demographics.** Socioeconomic class and household size differ between segments, but the effects are small, and age does not differ at all. A client could not have found these segments from demographics, which is exactly why XYZ's move to behavioural segmentation is worthwhile.

## Recommendations for XYZ's clients

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recommendations
#| tbl-cap: "One promotion approach per segment, from purchase behaviour (Question 2d) and demographics (Question 2e)."

recommendations <- tribble(
  ~segment, ~what_defines_it, ~recommended_approach,
  "Loyal regular-price buyers",
  "Most volume on one brand, almost no promotion buying",
  str_c("Reward and loyalty schemes to keep them; avoid discounts, which ",
        "only give away margin"),
  "Loyal promotion buyers",
  "The most loyal segment, and heavy users of other promotions",
  "Price promotions and value packs on the brand they already favour",
  "Heavy multi-brand shoppers",
  "The most volume and transactions, spread across many brands",
  str_c("Family and multi-packs tied to one brand, with rewards that ",
        "concentrate their spending"),
  "Promo-6 buyers",
  "Low loyalty, heavy use of promotion 6, more higher-class households",
  "Promotion 6 offers spread across the year; a cheaper product is not needed",
  "Small-brand regular-price buyers",
  str_c("Average volume, little spent on the eight named brands, rarely ",
        "buys on promotion"),
  str_c("Trial and visibility to win them from small brands; discounts are ",
        "unlikely to move them. The least sharply defined segment, so test ",
        "on a small scale first"),
  "Light occasional buyers",
  "Very low volume, few transactions, poorly recorded demographics",
  "Lowest priority for promotion spending"
) |>
  mutate(households = map_int(segment, seg_size), .after = segment)

recommendations |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(segment = "Segment", households = "Households",
             what_defines_it = "What defines it",
             recommended_approach = "Recommended approach") |>
  cols_width(segment ~ px(170), households ~ px(90))
```

The segments differ in *when* and *how* a promotion pays off, which is what lets a client spread several promotions across the year instead of one blanket discount. @tbl-recommendations sets out one approach per segment. The two loyal segments together hold `r seg_size("Loyal regular-price buyers") + seg_size("Loyal promotion buyers")` households, and they need opposite treatment: one should be rewarded without discounts, the other responds to discounts on its own brand. Treating them as one "loyal" group, as a demographic segmentation would, would waste the promotion budget on the first and under-serve the second.

## Limitations

- **The segments overlap.** The average silhouette width at six clusters is only `r sprintf("%.3f", k_compare$average_silhouette[k_compare$k == 6])`, and the adjusted Rand index against k-means is `r sprintf("%.3f", ari_kmeans)` (@sec-robust). The overlap is uneven: the average silhouette width is `r sprintf("%.3f", sil_strongest$width)` for the `r sil_strongest$segment` but only `r sprintf("%.3f", sil_weakest$width)` for the `r sil_weakest$segment`, so households near the borders of the weaker segments could reasonably belong to a neighbouring one.
- **Six groups is partly a judgement.** The silhouette slightly favours two groups; six was chosen because two would mix loyal and light buyers, which no client could act on (@sec-choose-k).
- **Data quality.** Demographics coded 0 were treated as missing, and `CHILD` = 5 was treated as an undocumented "not specified" code. `r nrow(share_exceptions)` households have brand shares that do not sum to 1, and the largest share of the `r hs0_n` households with no household size (and no education, language, gender, TV or Affluence) sits in the Light occasional segment.
- **Skewness in the promotion shares remains.** About half the households never use each promotion, so even after the square root the promotion shares stay skewed. This reflects real behaviour but makes those variables less symmetric than the others.
- **One sample, one period, no causation.** The analysis uses a subset of `r nrow(soap_raw)` households over a single period. The recommendations describe which promotion *fits* each segment's behaviour; they do not prove that a promotion *causes* a change, which only a controlled test could show.

## Next steps

1. Run the same segmentation on the full panel and on a later period, to check that the six segments are stable and to see which households move between them.
2. Test the recommended promotions with a controlled trial in one market before rolling them out, so their effect on each segment can be measured.
3. Consider a brand switching measure that is not built from `NoTrans`, which @sec-q2a showed is the problem with `BrandRuns` and `TransPerRun`, to capture the third view of loyalty in the brief.


# Appendix {#sec-appendix .unnumbered}

## Packages used {.unnumbered}

@tbl-appendix-package-versions records the installed versions of every package explicitly loaded in the shared setup, together with the rendering dependencies. These versions are read from the R library at execution time, rather than transcribed from a previous run. The complete attached-package and namespace information follows in `sessionInfo()`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-appendix-package-versions
#| tbl-cap: "R packages loaded by the shared setup and dependencies used for rendering."

# Keep this list aligned with the explicit package calls in the shared setup.
appendix_packages <- tibble(
  package = c("pacman", "tidyverse", "tidymodels", "here", "janitor", "gt",
              "scales", "patchwork", "factoextra", "cluster", "moments",
              "mclust",
              "knitr", "rmarkdown", "ragg"),
  role = c(rep("Shared setup", 12), rep("Rendering", 3))
) |>
  mutate(version = purrr::map_chr(package,
                                  \(pkg) as.character(packageVersion(pkg))))

appendix_packages |>
  select(package, version, role) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(package = "Package", version = "Installed version",
             role = "Use in this report")
```

The table identifies the computational environment used for this particular render. Matching these versions helps another reader investigate differences between runs, although a version table alone does not install or lock dependencies. R and Quarto versions are recorded in @sec-reproduce.
